decisions.evidence: Round 3 maker: “paste [a URL]… press Save bookmark”; round 3 client: “I pasted the link… and the card came back.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: saving a bookmark by entering its URL conforms.

decisions.evidence: Round 3 maker describes automatic “site identity, title, description, and address”; round 19 describes collected details as “title, description, and icon.” Round 3 client approves: “that’s exactly the feeling I was after,” without mentioning a preview image.
decisions.note: Prototype review: the presented automatic metadata set omits the required preview image. The client’s approval does not identify that difference.

decisions.evidence: Round 3 maker presents a card showing site identity, title, description, and address; round 9 maker adds labels visible on cards. Clients in rounds 3 and 9 confirm the cards are recognizable and labels are visible at a glance.
decisions.note: Prototype review: the accumulated card design exposes the required readability-first fields.

decisions.evidence: Round 3 maker presents the save result without an editing step; round 3 client requests that title and description be editable “both right there when I’m saving and later on.” Rounds 4–5 maker then presents both editing stages, which the client confirms.
decisions.note: Prototype review: the client surfaced and requested the missing before-and-after metadata editing behavior; the later clarification and disposition are linked as one decision.

decisions.evidence: Round 4 maker: “title and description are editable, while… the address remain[s] tied to the original page.” Round 4 client explicitly accepts that “the web address stay tied… not something I’d want to rewrite.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: the reference requires URL editing, but the client explicitly identified and accepted an immutable URL.

decisions.evidence: Rounds 4–5 maker limits wording edits to title and description; round 10 adds label editing. Round 31’s settled scope lists “editable wording” and labels but no note field or rendered markdown. The client approves the scope without mentioning notes.
decisions.note: Specification gate: the presented bookmark editor omits the required editable markdown note and its rendered view; the client does not surface the omission.

decisions.evidence: Rounds 4–5 maker presents editing title and description before and after saving; round 10 presents editing attached labels. The client confirms each behavior.
decisions.note: Prototype review: the presented title, description, and tag editing portions conform, independently of the URL and note divergences.

decisions.evidence: Round 6 maker: an exact repeat “should take you directly to the existing bookmark’s editor”; round 6 client confirms one updated card remains and no duplicate is created.
decisions.note: Prototype review: duplicate saving converges on editing the existing bookmark.

decisions.evidence: Round 7 maker defines search as covering “title, description, site name, and web address.” Round 7 client says those fields “all sound right,” without identifying the missing note field.
decisions.note: Prototype review: the explicitly enumerated full-text scope omits bookmark notes.

decisions.evidence: Round 7 maker presents live search without specifying capitalization behavior; round 7 client adds that it “shouldn’t care about capital letters.” Round 8 maker confirms and demonstrates that “Fluffy” returns the same result, which the client accepts.
decisions.note: Prototype review: the client supplied the missing case-insensitive requirement; the clarification and confirming presentation are one linked decision.

decisions.evidence: Round 9 maker asks the client to select Recipes and see only its two bookmarks; round 9 client confirms the list immediately narrows to those two.
decisions.note: Prototype review: selecting one tag filters to that tag’s bookmarks.

decisions.evidence: Round 9 maker presents filtering with sample labels; round 9 client requires user-created labels and says “a single bookmark should be able to carry more than one label.” Round 10 maker presents creating Weekend plans and retaining Recipes; the client confirms both.
decisions.note: Prototype review: the client extended the initial label presentation with the missing custom, multi-tag assignment behavior; later confirmation resolves the same decision.

decisions.evidence: Round 10 maker offers a plain type-in version and a picker that displays existing labels. The client selects the picker because it “shows me the labels I already have” and avoids near-duplicates.
decisions.note: Prototype review: the alternatives differed on existing-tag suggestions, and the client selected the reference-conforming autocomplete/picker alternative.

decisions.evidence: Round 11 maker presents the label picker during initial saving, allowing Recipes and Weekend plans together; round 11 client confirms both appear on the saved card.
decisions.note: Prototype review: the revised save flow supports assigning multiple tags when the bookmark is created.

decisions.evidence: Round 12 maker presents marking a card Read later and selecting a dedicated Read later collection filter; round 12 client confirms the flag is visible and the filtered view contains the expected cards.
decisions.note: Prototype review: marking unread/read-later and viewing that subset conform.

decisions.evidence: Round 12 maker states Read later is reversible; after the client asks to confirm removal, round 13 maker demonstrates unchecking it and the card disappearing from the focused view. Round 13 client accepts.
decisions.note: Prototype review: the clarification resolves to the required mark-as-read/removal behavior without a divergent presentation.

decisions.evidence: Round 14 maker presents confirmed deletion that removes the card immediately; round 14 client confirms the card vanished and understands it as permanent removal.
decisions.note: Prototype review: permanent bookmark deletion conforms.

decisions.evidence: Round 14 maker presents permanent deletion only; round 14 client says it must differ from “tucking something out of sight” and expects that case separately. Round 18 maker then presents reversible archive, exclusion from the everyday list/search, a separate Archived view, and Restore; the client confirms all of it.
decisions.note: Prototype review: the client surfaced the missing archive-versus-delete lifecycle; the later archive presentation is the disposition of that pending decision.

decisions.evidence: Round 15 maker presents selecting two bookmarks and bulk deleting them with a selected count and confirmation; round 15 client confirms the collection drops from six to four.
decisions.note: Prototype review: multi-selection and bulk deletion conform.

decisions.evidence: Round 15 maker initially presents bulk deletion; round 15 client adds that the same selection must support adding a label and marking several items Read later. Rounds 16–17 maker presents both actions, and the client confirms them.
decisions.note: Prototype review: the client extended the initially narrow batch action set with two required non-delete actions; the subsequent demonstrations resolve that request.

decisions.evidence: Rounds 15–17 maker repeatedly demonstrates bulk actions after manually selecting individual cards. Neither the presentations nor client responses establish whether an action can target the entire collection matching the current filter.
decisions.note: Prototype/specification review: the record establishes selected-item bulk actions but leaves filter-wide bulk targeting undecided, so divergence cannot be determined.

decisions.evidence: Round 22 maker presents case-insensitive reuse of an existing Recipes tag rather than creating a duplicate; the client initially requests visible proof. Round 23 maker supplies the reuse-message and saved-card states, and the client confirms “two labels, no… lowercase duplicate.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: the pending visual clarification is linked to its final disposition; unique-tag reuse conforms.

decisions.evidence: Round 24 maker presents display-only truncation that keeps cards aligned while preserving complete values for editing; round 24 client accepts because the collection remains scannable and no data is discarded.
decisions.note: Prototype review: display shortening preserves the readability-first list and underlying bookmark content.

decisions.evidence: Round 25 maker proposes treating tracking suffixes and section fragments as the same bookmark while preserving meaningful URL differences; round 25 client explicitly agrees with that boundary.
decisions.note: Prototype review: this is a conforming duplicate-prevention refinement, not a departure from the duplicate rule.

decisions.evidence: Round 27 maker presents an empty Read later shelf while retaining search, labels, and a route to all bookmarks; round 27 client confirms this correctly represents an empty subset of a nonempty collection.
decisions.note: Prototype review: the separate unread view has a coherent empty state and route back.

decisions.evidence: Round 28 maker offers archived-duplicate behaviors; the client selects the version that opens the existing archived record, creates no duplicate, clearly reports its archived state, and restores only on an explicit action.
decisions.note: Prototype review: duplicate convergence respects the archive state and separate archive view.

decisions.evidence: Round 30 maker says opening a retained bookmark “would still try the original address”; round 30 client agrees that it should still try that address even if the site now errors.
decisions.note: Prototype review: opening a bookmark navigates to its original URL.

decisions.evidence: Round 30 client explicitly asks that saving “keep its own copy of the page” so dead links remain readable. Round 31 maker defers preservation to a later cycle; round 31 client says she is “content with keeping the ‘saved copy of the page’ idea… for a later round.” Round 32 repeats and accepts the deferral.
decisions.note: Specification gate through implementation review: the client identified the missing local snapshot behavior and explicitly accepted its deferral. The repeated final confirmation is linked to the same decision, not double-counted.

decisions.evidence: Round 31 client states that “sorting of the list” matters in the real collection. Round 32 maker says the app uses fixed “newest-saved-first ordering” and that user-controlled sorting remains for later; the client says she still wants it but is comfortable deferring it.
decisions.note: Implementation review: the client explicitly recognized that selectable sorting was absent and accepted the fixed-order implementation for this cycle.
